summary: Defines terms used when measuring the performance of firewalls, extending the vocabulary already used for benchmarking routers and switches. It is informational.

plainLanguage.summary: A dictionary of words so everyone means the same thing when they say how fast or sturdy a network guard gate is.

questions: what is a dmz in networking
subtitle: A shared vocabulary for measuring how fast and how well firewalls forward traffic.

tldr.problem: There was no standard way to measure firewall performance, products differ widely, and buyers could not tell whether a firewall would cope with heavy loads on fast internal networks.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC defines 33 terms, from allowed traffic and bit forwarding rate to concurrent connections and unit of transfer, extending the router and switch benchmarking vocabulary.
tldr.outcome: It supplies definitions only, not test methods. It also warns that the best performance setting may not be the most secure one.

today: RFC 2647 is an Informational RFC and no later RFC is listed as obsoleting or updating it. It defines terms only and does not give a test methodology.

sections.title: Why Firewall Terms Are Needed
sections.content:
RFC 2647 defines terms for measuring firewall performance. It extends the vocabulary already used for benchmarking routers (RFC 1242 and RFC 2544) and switches (RFC 2285). Forwarding rate and connection-oriented measurements are the main metrics.

The author gives three reasons. There was no standard method of measurement. Implementations vary widely, so direct comparison is hard. And firewalls were being deployed on fast internal networks, even though most were tuned for slow wide-area links. Buyers were often unsure whether a product would stand up to heavy loads.
sections.plainLanguage: People bought gates for their networks without a fair way to compare them. This document first agrees on the words so a fair test can follow.

sections.title: Definition Format and Reuse
sections.content:
Each term follows the format from RFC 1242: a definition, a discussion, measurement units (optional), issues (optional) and cross-references. Readers are told to consult the router and switch documents first, because they discuss several terms that also matter for firewalls.

The device being tested is called the DUT/SUT, the device under test or system under test. Some terms deliberately differ from the older documents. For example, bit forwarding rate here counts only allowed traffic and counts bits per second rather than frames per second.
sections.plainLanguage: Every word gets the same set of boxes to fill: what it means, why it matters and what to compare it with. The tested gate is simply called the thing under test.

sections.title: Kinds of Firewalls and Traffic
sections.content:
A firewall is a device or group of devices that enforces an access control policy between networks. The RFC distinguishes several designs. Packet filtering looks at packet headers. Stateful packet filtering forwards only packets that match state the device keeps for each connection. A circuit proxy statically forwards whatever its rule set permits, while an application proxy is set up and torn down in response to a client request.

Traffic is split into classes. Allowed traffic is forwarded because of the rule set. Rejected traffic is packets actually dropped. Illegal traffic is everything the rule set specifies for rejection, so a buggy firewall might forward some of it. Only allowed traffic counts toward forwarding rate.
sections.plainLanguage: Some guards check each visitor's ticket, some remember who already came in, and some go out and shake hands on your behalf. Visitors are sorted into let in, turned away, and should-have-been-turned-away.

sections.title: Network Zones and Interfaces
sections.content:
A protected network is a segment whose access the firewall controls. An unprotected network is one it does not control. A demilitarized zone (DMZ) sits between them and may hold public servers such as HTTP or FTP. The number of logical interfaces is called how many ways the firewall is homed, so a firewall with three interfaces is tri-homed.

The RFC notes that a tri-homed firewall may offer security advantages: an attacker who compromises hosts on the DMZ still cannot reach hosts on the protected network. It discourages test setups with one physical interface and several logical ones, because leakage between segments is hard to rule out. A policy is the document that says what access is acceptable, and the rule set is the collection of rules that enforces it.
sections.plainLanguage: Picture a castle: the inside, the outside, and a courtyard between them. A guard who watches all three areas is tri-homed.

sections.title: Measuring Rates and Connections
sections.content:
Bit forwarding rate is the bits per second of allowed traffic the device is observed to transmit to the correct destination interface for a given offered load. It is a goodput measure: bits lost or retransmitted are subtracted. A unit of transfer (UOT) is a discrete collection of bytes with at least one header, such as a TCP segment, IP packet, Ethernet frame or ATM cell. Testers must say which UOT they use and compare only like UOTs.

A connection is a state in which two hosts, or a host and the device, agree to exchange data. UDP exchanges count for this purpose. The RFC defines concurrent connections, connection establishment time, connection teardown time and connection overhead. Steady-state forwarding must be measured after establishment and security associations are complete and before teardown begins. Logging, authentication and network address translation can all add cost, and the RFC says testers should not measure performance in terms of users supported.
sections.plainLanguage: To time a gate fairly, count only the people actually let through, and start the stopwatch after the handshake is done. Compare apples with apples.

sections.title: Security and Performance Trade-offs
sections.content:
The memo warns that the best configuration for performance may not be the most secure, and the reverse. Some attacks hurt performance: a denial-of-service attack can bombard a firewall with so much rejected traffic that it cannot forward allowed traffic, and even a small amount of traffic may degrade or stop a firewall. Defences against such attacks can themselves cost performance.

No specific attacks are defined, since the library of attacks keeps growing. The RFC says a reasonable benchmark should consider safeguards against them, and the same safeguards should be in place when comparing different firewalls.
sections.plainLanguage: A gate that is fastest may leave the lock open. Keep the same locks on every gate when you race them.

items.title: Allowed traffic
items.text: Packets forwarded as a result of the rule set. Counted in forwarding rate.

items.title: Rejected traffic
items.text: Packets actually dropped because of the rule set. Not counted.

items.title: Illegal traffic
items.text: All packets the rule set says to reject, whether or not they were dropped.
